query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐chromium steels used in chemical‐processing and nuclear‐power applications, the intrinsic resistance to corrosion is primarily governed by the formation and rapid regeneration of a chromium‐rich passive oxide layer (mainly Cr2O3) on the steel surface.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels with sufficient chromium content and a naturally formed, continuous passive oxide film in a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of identical steel samples: one retaining the naturally formed oxide layer and one where the oxide layer is deliberately removed (via mechanical polishing and/or chemical cleaning) to disrupt passivation, then expose both groups to a simulated corrosive environment.
generation.conditions: Controlled laboratory tests that simulate chemical-processing and nuclear service environments (e.g., aqueous chloride or similar corrosive media at moderate to elevated temperatures where diffusion processes remain active and oxygen levels allow passive film regeneration).
generation.structural_mediator: The presence and integrity of a chromium‐rich (Cr2O3) passive film that forms or reforms on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Under corrosive conditions, chromium within the steel rapidly oxidizes along active sites, such as grain boundaries, to form a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 film that acts as a barrier to ion and electron transport. In samples with an intact or rapidly regenerating passive film, this barrier minimizes further corrosion, whereas removal of the film disrupts this protection.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples that retain or quickly regenerate the Cr2O3 passive layer will display significantly lower corrosion rates (evidenced by reduced weight loss and lower electrochemical corrosion current densities) compared to samples in which the passive film is removed and reformation is hindered.
generation.baseline: Standard high‐chromium steels under identical exposure conditions that have an intact natural passive film.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels with adequate chromium content and under corrosive conditions that do not aggressively disrupt the passive film (e.g., environments with moderate chloride concentrations and temperatures within the range conducive to diffusion-driven passivation). It may not apply in extreme environments where other degradation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The degree to which microstructural variations (e.g., grain size differences) or the presence of minor alloying elements affect the kinetics of film reformation remains to be fully quantified, especially under conditions more aggressive than those simulated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high‐chromium steel samples with identical composition and microstructure. For Group 1, leave the native oxide intact. For Group 2, remove the oxide layer by mechanical polishing followed by chemical cleaning. Expose both groups to a corrosive medium (e.g., an aqueous chloride solution) at a controlled temperature for a fixed duration. Use surface analysis techniques (XPS/SEM) to monitor passive film formation and standard corrosion measurements (weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) to assess corrosion rates.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to determine corrosion current densities
Surface composition and film thickness analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion rates (weight loss and electrochemical responses) of samples with the intact passive film and those with the removed film do not differ significantly, or if the cleaned samples rapidly reform a passive film that is compositionally indistinguishable from the intact film without an associated improvement in corrosion resistance, then the hypothesis that the corrosion resistance is primarily due to the formation and regeneration of the Cr2O3 passive layer would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].

drafts.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the formation of a continuous, self-healing chromium oxide film that passivates the metal surface against aggressive environments.
drafts.material_initial_state: Commercially available low-alloy/stainless steel containing at least 12 wt% chromium (with typical additions of nickel and possibly molybdenum) in its as-fabricated condition with a naturally formed thin oxide layer.
drafts.intervention: Deliberate removal of the native oxide layer (e.g., by mechanical polishing or mild chemical etching) followed by controlled re-exposure to a corrosive environment to trigger repassivation.
drafts.conditions: Samples exposed to environments simulating chemical-processing conditions (e.g., acidic or saline solutions at moderate temperatures) and, where feasible, conditions mimicking operational parameters (e.g., temperature, radiation flux) of nuclear-power applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: A nanometer-scale, crystalline chromium oxide (Cr2O3) layer that forms uniformly on the steel surface, potentially aided by the presence of other alloying elements that stabilize its structure.
drafts.mechanism: Upon oxide removal, the exposed chromium in the alloy preferentially oxidizes to form a thin, adherent Cr2O3 film. This film acts as a barrier to the ingress of corrosive species by limiting oxygen and ion diffusion, thereby significantly reducing the overall corrosion rate. In addition, the film is self-healing when minor disruptions occur, which maintains long-term corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Steel samples that undergo controlled re-passivation will rapidly reform a protective chromium oxide film and exhibit significantly lower rates of corrosion (as measured by weight loss and surface degradation) compared to samples where the film is intentionally disrupted or not allowed to reform.
drafts.baseline: Steel samples with the naturally formed, intact passivating oxide layer exhibiting standard corrosion resistance under identical test conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels with sufficient chromium content (around or above 12 wt%) under the specific environmental conditions used in the test (e.g., specific pH, temperature, and radiation levels relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear applications). It may not apply to steels with insufficient passivating element content or to environments where other corrosion mechanisms dominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of steel samples with the specified alloy composition. Divide them into three groups: (1) untouched native oxide; (2) oxide removed followed by immediate re-exposure under controlled corrosive conditions to allow re-passivation; (3) oxide removed and maintained in an inert atmosphere to prevent re-passivation. Expose all samples to a standardized corrosive environment (e.g., acidic saline solution at a controlled temperature). Periodically measure corrosion rates using weight loss measurements, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and post-exposure surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to evaluate the presence and integrity of the chromium oxide layer.
measurements: Weight loss over time as an index of overall corrosion rate
Electrochemical impedance spectra to assess the protective nature of surface films
Surface morphology and composition (using SEM/EDS or XPS) to confirm the reformation and uniformity of the chromium oxide film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the re-passivated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate compared to the baseline intact oxide samples or if post-exposure surface characterization fails to confirm the formation of a continuous chromium oxide film, then the hypothesis that the self-healing chromium oxide layer is the primary mechanism behind corrosion resistance would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the formation of a chromium-rich passive oxide layer that impedes the attack of corrosive species.
drafts.material_initial_state: Steels with a homogeneous microstructure containing alloyed chromium, where a natural passive oxide layer (rich in chromium oxides) is present on the surface.
drafts.intervention: Expose two sets of identical steel samples—one with the naturally formed passive oxide layer intact and one where the oxide layer is removed by mechanical polishing and chemical cleaning—to simulated corrosive environments.
drafts.conditions: Test samples in environments that mimic operational conditions such as elevated temperatures, acidic or chloride-containing solutions (reflective of chemical-processing and nuclear-power settings), while maintaining consistent pH, temperature, and chloride concentration.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and maintenance of a chromium-rich (primarily Cr2O3) passive oxide film on the steel surface.
drafts.mechanism: Under corrosive conditions, chromium within the steel oxidizes to form a compact and adherent Cr2O3 layer. This passive film slows down the transport of corrosive ions (e.g., Cl-) to the underlying metal, thereby reducing the rate of metal dissolution and corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Steel samples that retain the intact chromium-rich passive oxide layer will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates (e.g., as measured by weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) compared to samples from which the oxide layer was removed.
drafts.baseline: Corrosion behavior of similar steel samples with the naturally formed oxide layer intact under identical exposure conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels with sufficient chromium content under controlled corrosive environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power operations. However, extreme conditions (e.g., very high temperatures, highly aggressive pH, or unusually high chloride concentrations) may overwhelm the protective effect of the passive film.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of steel coupons with identical alloy compositions. Remove the surface oxide from one group using mechanical polishing and chemical cleaning. Expose both groups to a corrosive environment that simulates operational conditions (e.g., elevated temperature, acidic chloride solution). Periodically assess corrosion using weight loss measurements, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and surface analysis (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) to monitor the oxide layer's composition.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion rates of the steel samples with and without the initial oxide layer are statistically indistinguishable, or if the reformed oxide on the cleaned samples is not enriched in chromium relative to the samples with the intact initial oxide, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high‐chromium stainless steels used in chemical‐processing and nuclear-power applications, the intrinsic corrosion resistance derives from the rapid segregation and diffusion of chromium to the surface via grain boundaries, which promotes the formation of a thin, adherent, and self-healing Cr2O3 passivation film that inhibits further oxidation and metal loss.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-chromium stainless steel with a controlled composition (including minor additions such as Mn) exhibiting a fine-grained microstructure that facilitates fast grain boundary diffusion.
drafts.intervention: Systematically vary the steel’s grain size (through heat treatment) and adjust minor alloying elements that could affect Cr diffusion, then expose the samples to corrosive environments (e.g., aqueous chloride solutions or molten salts typical of nuclear service conditions).
drafts.conditions: Testing in a controlled laboratory setup simulating chemical-processing or nuclear-power environments—temperatures up to about 700°C where diffusion remains significant and corrosive species (e.g., chloride ions or salt impurities) are present under steady-state service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The density of grain boundaries and the distribution of Cr within the microstructure mediate the kinetics of Cr diffusion to the surface and, consequently, the formation and renewal of the Cr2O3 passive film.
drafts.mechanism: Under corrosive conditions, Cr diffuses preferentially along grain boundaries to the steel surface, where it oxidizes to form a continuous Cr2O3 film. This passive film provides a barrier to further corrosion by limiting electron transfer and metal dissolution. A decrease in grain-boundary density or a disruption in the alloy’s ability to effectively supply Cr will impair film formation and compromise corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples with a fine-grained microstructure and enhanced Cr diffusion (due to optimal alloying and heat treatment) will develop a more uniform and stable Cr2O3 film and exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates than coarse-grained or compositionally modified steels that impede Cr migration. Relative to a baseline of coarse-grained or lower-Cr steels, improved corrosion resistance should be observed via lower weight loss, reduced corrosion current densities, and thicker, continuous passive films by surface analysis.
drafts.baseline: Standard stainless steels with relatively coarse grains and lower effective Cr diffusion under identical testing conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis should hold in environments where the passive film is not aggressively attacked (e.g., moderate chloride concentrations or controlled molten salt conditions) and at service temperatures where diffusion processes remain active (up to about 700°C). It may not apply if external factors (such as severe mechanical stress or extreme chemical environments) overwhelm the passive film's stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-chromium steel samples by controlling grain size (fine vs. coarse) and modifying the alloy composition to selectively inhibit or enhance Cr diffusion (e.g., by varying Mn content). Subject these samples to identical corrosive environments that mimic chemical-processing and nuclear service conditions. Monitor the formation and stability of the Cr2O3 passivation layer via surface analysis (XPS, SEM) and measure corrosion rates using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and weight-loss methods.
measurements: Grain size and microstructural characterization (e.g., via SEM/EBSD)
Surface film composition and thickness (via XPS)
Corrosion rate (weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Uniformity and continuity of the Cr2O3 film (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the variation in grain size or alloying that is expected to enhance Cr diffusion does not result in a statistically significant improvement in the formation or stability of the Cr2O3 film (or if no corresponding reduction in corrosion rate is observed) compared with the baseline, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In corrosion‐resistant steels for chemical processing and nuclear power applications, a thin, chromium‐enriched passive film forms on the surface that continuously regenerates under corrosive conditions and acts as a barrier to further material degradation. Minor elements such as aluminum can enhance this protection by sacrificially oxidizing and buffering the environment, thereby reducing the dissolution of chromium.
drafts.material_initial_state: Austenitic or ferritic stainless steels with a nominal high chromium content (and optionally minor aluminum additions) in the as-manufactured state, presenting a homogeneous bulk composition with the potential for surface passive film formation.
drafts.intervention: Expose samples of standard corrosion‐resistant steel and modified variants with reduced chromium or altered aluminum content to a controlled corrosive environment representative of chemical-processing/nuclear conditions (e.g., high-temperature chloride or molten salt media, or simulated nuclear coolant environments) and monitor passive film formation and stability.
drafts.conditions: Testing performed at temperatures and chemical potentials representative of operating conditions (for example, temperatures up to 300–700 °C in a corrosive aqueous or molten salt environment) with controlled oxygen levels and flow rates; baseline measurements of corrosion rates and passive film characteristics under non-corrosive (inert) reference conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and sustained integrity of a Cr-rich oxide layer (primarily Cr2O3) at the metal surface; any sacrificial oxidation of minor elements (e.g., aluminum forming Al2O3) contributing to redox buffering that reduces Cr dissolution.
drafts.mechanism: The high Cr content leads to preferential oxidation that forms a dense, adherent passive oxide film. Under exposure to corrosive agents, this film regenerates in situ, while minor alloying elements (if present) oxidize first, reducing local aggressive attack and preserving the Cr enrichment. This combined effect slows down overall material degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline steel with standard Cr content, steels with reduced Cr (or without the beneficial minor elements) will exhibit faster corrosion rates, greater Cr depletion in the surface oxide (as measured by XPS or similar techniques), and inferior passive film stability. In control samples with standard composition, the passive film should maintain a lower corrosion current density and lower overall mass loss over time.
drafts.baseline: Standard corrosion‐resistant steel (e.g., an AISI 304 or DS2205 duplex steel) exhibiting well-documented corrosion resistance through a stable Cr-rich passive film under similar exposure conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels operating under aggressive chemical-processing and nuclear conditions where oxidation/reduction potentials allow for passive film formation. It may not apply in environments that either excessively oxidize or completely inhibit passive film regeneration, or in systems where entirely different mechanisms (e.g., irradiation-induced microstructural changes) dominate corrosion behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of steel samples with systematically varied chromium and minor (e.g., aluminum) content. Expose these samples under identical controlled conditions in a representative corrosive medium (e.g., a high-temperature chloride or molten salt solution). Use identical test setups (electrochemical cells, temperature, flow conditions) with appropriate inert controls. Surface analysis (XPS, SEM) of the passive film and bulk corrosion rates (via weight loss and/or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) will be performed at multiple time points.
measurements: Corrosion rate (mass loss per unit area)
Composition and thickness of the passive oxide film (via XPS, TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with a reduced chromium content (or without minor sacrificial elements) show corrosion resistance (low corrosion rates, stable and compositionally similar passive films) that is statistically indistinguishable from that of the standard corrosion‐resistant steel under the same conditions, then the hypothesized mechanism of a protective Cr-rich passive film (and its enhancement by minor elements) would be falsified.
